doc.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How Glad I Am, the r-and-b Grammy, and the jazz label
summary: She recorded How Glad I Am against advice, won the r-and-b Grammy, and now accepts being called a jazz singer.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: By ’64, when you won a Grammy, How Glad I Am . . .
Which nobody wanted me to record, except me.
They thought it was too r-and-b.
And it in fact did win in . . .
It won the r-and-b Grammy. “No, this is not you.” “Well, I’m sorry. I like the song, and I’m singing it.”
I have no idea. I don’t think so. How Glad I Am. It wasn’t Gerald Wilson. Oliver Nelson, maybe? [It was Sid Feller.]
That I’d have to look up. I’m not sure.
I don’t know. I should know that. See, that’s – I really should know that. I don’t.
Did you think – what did you think about the fact that it was “r-and-b”?

I didn’t think anything about it. I sing what I want to sing. I just sing songs. That whole – that’s why I say song stylist. Everybody else goes someplace else. I just sing songs, and I don’t put a label on them.
But do you care that other people do?
All right. Do you object to being called a jazz singer?
Not today. I’m 73 years old. I’m black. What else am I going to be? I’ve outlived my pop days. Still singing the same songs the same way as I did 40 years ago, and today it’s jazz.
